newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: WTO deal sets stage for free trade in infotech.
newsitem.headline: WTO deal sets stage for free trade in infotech.

text.p: Twenty-eight countries agreed on Friday to a pact to eliminate tariffs on a range of high-technology products from computers to telephone headsets by the year 2000.
The deal, at the end of the week-long inaugural ministerial conference of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) in Singapore, will cut tariffs in four stages between 1997 and 2000.
Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said the 28 countries represented 84 percent of global trade in the booming information technology sector.
With another six countries committed to signing the deal soon, the information technology agreement (ITA) would cover over 90 percent of such global trade, guaranteeing its success.
Inclusion of 90 percent of the trade had been the key hurdle set by the European Union (EU) and the United States for implementation of the information technology agreement (ITA).
"Criterion number one -- do we have approximately 90 percent of trade covered? We are already there," Barshefsky told a news conference on the final day of the week-long meeting.
The WTO estimates world exports of information technology products totalled around $600 billion in 1995. Analysts say the sector is growing by at least 15 percent annually.
Japanese Vice Trade Minister Hiroshi Hosokawa said agreement on the pact was one of the most important achievements of the WTO meeting and would benefit consumers around the world by cutting prices.
"We now live in an information age," he told Reuters. "Information technology products have started to be used in every corner of our lives."
Computer software giant Microsoft Corp hailed the deal as "win-win for every country and every consumer".
"The agreement will mean lower costs and greater access to innovation and technology for consumers in every nation around the world," it said in a statement.
Canadian Trade Minister Art Eggleton welcomed the agreement, saying it would contribute to economic growth and create jobs. "This agreement is a red-letter day," he said.
Barshefsky said the ITA allowed countries to remove tariffs before 2000 if they wished.
"It would be our hope that at a minimum we (the United States) and the European Union would accelerate our tariff cuts. "We would not wait until the year 2000 to go to zero."
European officials earlier said that agreement on an ITA depended on countries representing about 90 percent of world trade in information technology joining the pact by March 15, 1997.
They said the ITA, reached after four days of intense, round-the-clock talks, marked the most far-reaching agreement ever towards free trade in a single sector.

The deal covers the bulk of industrial information technology products, as well as digital photocopiers and capacitors -- circuits used in electronic equipment-- while excluding consumer electronics and audio materials.
EU Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan called the ITA "a huge advance for the world economy".
"It will be good for the IT industry, and will act as a catalyst for industrial growth," Brittan said.

The 28 countries that have signed up include the 15 EU members and the United States. The others are Australia, Canada, Hong Kong, Iceland, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Norway, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan and Turkey.
Japanese officials said they expected Malaysia, New Zealand and the Philippines to join the deal over the next few months.
